verses.note: The blessing goes to Shem through his God. Genesis will trace the chosen line from Shem to Abram (11:10-26), and here the reader learns that what sets that line apart is the LORD who has attached himself to it.
The promise is now specified: not any son of Abraham, but Sarah's son. God's choice of the line through which his purpose runs is his own, which Paul develops in Romans 9:7-9.

The distinction between Ishmael and Isaac is not about merit; neither is yet born to the covenant line, and one is not yet born at all. Paul reads it as showing that God's purpose rests on promise (Romans 9:7-9, Galatians 4:28).

The verse is one of the clearest statements of election's purpose in the Old Testament. God's choice of Abraham is a free act of personal commitment, and it aims at a people who do righteousness and justice. Election is for a task, not for privilege alone.

The inheritance runs through one son, not both. The verse is the human side of what God will confirm in verse 12, and Paul later builds on it to show that the promise, not natural descent, determines who belongs to God's people (Romans 9:7-8).

Abraham has many sons but one heir of the promise. The other sons are not cursed or cast off without provision; they are given gifts and a future. The verse shows that God's choice of one line to carry the promise does not mean contempt for the others.

The oracle speaks of nations and of which brother will carry the line, and Christians differ on how far Paul extends it to the salvation of individuals. Augustinian and Reformed readers take Romans 9 to teach individual election grounded only in God's mercy; Arminian and many other readers take it to concern God's freedom to choose the people and line through which he works. Both agree the choice is not earned.

God's attention settles on the one who is not chosen by Jacob. The pattern of God choosing the overlooked, already seen in the choice of Isaac over Ishmael and of Jacob himself over Esau, runs here through a woman, and from her come Levi and Judah.

The name that God gives Jacob becomes the name of the chosen people. Election in Genesis is not a reward for good character; it is God's commitment to a flawed man, marked by a name that describes his struggle rather than his virtue.

The twelve are named as a set, children of four mothers and of a divided household, and every one becomes a tribe of Israel. God's choosing does not wait for a tidy family; it forms a people out of the one that exists.

Again the younger comes before the older, as with Jacob and Esau and later Ephraim and Manasseh (48:14). God's choice of the line runs past the arrangements people make to secure the firstborn's place, even the thread tied on a wrist.

Seventy people are all the chosen family amounts to at this point. Deuteronomy 10:22 looks back on the number to make the point that Israel's growth was God's doing, not its own strength (compare Deuteronomy 7:7).

The right hand goes to the younger by the patriarch's deliberate act. Genesis has repeatedly shown God's choice running against birth order (Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Perez, Joseph); here that pattern is enacted openly, with no deceit, as a matter of the blessing's content.

God's choice of Levi from all the tribes is an election to service. Deuteronomy uses the same verb, bachar, for God's choice of Israel (7:6) and of the place of worship (12:5): being chosen means being set apart for a task.
David's standing before God rests on being known and chosen. He appeals to nothing in himself, only to God's word and purpose.

The love that chose Israel in the first place (Deuteronomy 7:7-8) is the same love that draws them back. Election in the Old Testament is God's persistent love for a people, and this verse shows it surviving judgment.

God's choice of Israel does not finally depend on Israel's record. Paul draws the same conclusion when he says that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable and that Israel remains beloved for the patriarchs' sake (Romans 11:28-29). How that election is fulfilled, in the church or in a future turning of ethnic Israel or both, is a second-order question Christians answer differently.
Jesus sees and calls. The initiative is entirely his; the disciples do not apply. The pattern matches God's calling of prophets and of Israel itself.
Jesus calls those he wants. The initiative is entirely his, as the choice of Israel was God's (Deuteronomy 7:6-8), and the chosen include a tax collector, fishermen, and the one who will betray him.

God's choosing is here a source of protection: he limits the suffering for the sake of his chosen people. Christians differ on the grounds of election (God's free decision or his foreknowledge of faith), but the verse's own point is God's care for those who are his.
The elect are gathered by the Son of Man and belong to him. Election in this chapter ends in gathering, not only in protection.
Mary is addressed by what God has done for her before anything she does. The verse presents God's choice as free favor, given to a young woman of no standing in a village of no reputation.

Descent from Abraham does not guarantee a place among his children. God can raise children for Abraham from stones, which anticipates the inclusion of the Gentiles and Paul's argument that Abraham's true children are those who share his faith (Romans 4:16, Galatians 3:7).
Israel's election is not a fence against God's mercy to others. The Scriptures Nazareth honored already record God choosing a Gentile general for healing while Israel's own sufferers waited.
Jesus chooses; the Twelve do not volunteer. Luke uses the same verb when he recalls the apostles ‘whom He had chosen’ in Acts 1:2.

‘To whom He wishes’ has been cited in debates about God's choice in salvation. Reformed interpreters read it as the Son's sovereign will in giving life; others note that the next verses name those who receive life as those who hear and believe (verse 24). Both readings agree that the Son is not an agent acting under constraint but gives life freely.

The verse speaks of a people given to the Son by the Father and certain to come. Reformed interpreters read it as a statement of unconditional election; Arminian and Wesleyan readers take the giving to follow God's foreknowledge of faith, or to describe believers as a class. Both read the second half as an unqualified welcome: no one who comes is refused. The chapter note's hard question sets out the debate.

Coming to Christ is not something people achieve by their own insight: the Father must draw them. Augustine read this drawing as the attraction of delight rather than compulsion (Tractates on John 26). How far the drawing is effective in itself, and whether it reaches all, divides Reformed, Lutheran, Arminian, Catholic, and Orthodox teaching.

Jesus explains unbelief among his followers by returning to the Father's giving (6:37, 44). The verse is meant to account for defection, not to discourage the anxious: the Father's gift makes coming possible, and the one who comes is not cast out.

Jesus' choosing of the Twelve includes Judas. The verse shows that being chosen for an office or a place near Jesus is not the same as belonging to him in faith; Jesus chose Judas knowingly (6:64), and Judas remained responsible for his betrayal.

Jesus traces belief to belonging: the sheep believe because they are his sheep. Augustinian and Reformed readers see here the Father's prior giving of the sheep to the Son (6:37, 10:29). Others, including Arminian readers, stress that the hearers are responsible for their unbelief and that the verse describes the present state of these opponents, not a fixed decree. Both read the verse as denying that unbelief is merely a lack of evidence.

Jesus' choice of the Twelve included Judas, and Jesus knew it (6:70-71). John does not explain how divine choosing and human betrayal fit together; he insists that the betrayal fell within the Father's purpose revealed in Scripture and that Judas remained responsible.

Jesus' choice of the disciples is the ground of their life and their fruitfulness. In John the choosing is always for a purpose, to go and bear fruit, and it includes Judas (6:70), so the Gospel holds together divine initiative and the call to remain. Reformed interpreters read the verse as a statement of God's sovereign choosing; Arminian interpreters read it as Jesus' choice of the Twelve for their apostolic task. Both agree that the initiative in the relationship is his.
The disciples are distinguished from the world not by their own superiority but by Jesus' choice. Being chosen out of the world does not remove them from it (17:15) but changes whom they belong to.

Those who receive eternal life are described as the Father's gift to the Son, a theme first heard in 6:37-39. Augustinian and Reformed interpreters read this as the Father's sovereign choice of a people for his Son; Arminian and many other interpreters read the given as those whom the Father draws and who respond in faith, known to God in advance. Both readings agree that salvation originates in the Father's giving and is secured by the Son's giving of life.

The good shepherd ‘calls his own sheep by name’ and they know his voice (10:3-4, 10:14). Mary's recognition is the fulfillment of that saying: the risen Lord knows his own personally, and faith is born in hearing him speak one's name.
The promise is universal in reach and rests on God's call. Christians differ on how that call relates to human response, but the verse places God's summons at the source of the church's growth.

The verse is central to the doctrine of election. Augustinian and Reformed readers (Calvin, the Canons of Dort, 1619) take foreknowledge as God's prior choosing love, which causes faith; Arminian readers (Jacobus Arminius, John Wesley's sermon On Predestination, which takes these two verses as its text) take it as God's knowledge of who would believe; Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics II/2, 1942) read election first as God's choosing of Jesus Christ, in whom a people is chosen. All agree that the goal of election is likeness to Christ.

The distinction between Israel and the Israel of promise introduces the theme of election. Readings divide from here: whether the chapter concerns individuals chosen for salvation, the formation of a people and its role in history, or both.

The choice of Isaac shows that God's promise was never simply a matter of descent. Paul's first example involves two sons of one father by different mothers; the next (verses 10-13) removes even that difference.
By choosing an example with one father, one mother, and one conception, Paul removes every natural ground for the distinction God made. Whatever election means, it is not based on ancestry.

These verses are the classic text for unconditional election. Augustine's reply To Simplician (396) worked through Romans 9:10-29 and concluded that God's choice precedes and causes faith, a reading Calvin and the Canons of Dort (1619) followed. Arminian readers answer that Paul excludes works, not faith, and that the choice concerns Jacob and Esau as heads of nations and their roles in history, as Genesis 25:23 says. John Piper's The Justification of God (1983) is a detailed modern defense of the individual reading; William Klein's The New Chosen People (1990) and Brian Abasciano's studies of Romans 9 argue for corporate election.

Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics II/2 (1942), read Romans 9-11 as describing the one elect community in two forms: Israel, which reflects the judgment God took upon himself in Christ, and the church, which reflects his mercy. For Barth, Jesus Christ is both the electing God and the elected man, the rejected one and the chosen one, and vessels of wrath and mercy are both held within God's purpose in him. Barth's reading is a distinct fourth position beside the Augustinian, Arminian, and corporate readings.

God's choice of his people is in Christ and before creation. The Reformed tradition (Augustine, Calvin's Institutes 3.21-24, the Synod of Dort, 1618-19) reads it as God's unconditional choice of particular persons; the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions read it as choice grounded in God's foreknowledge of faith; Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics II/2, 1942) read Christ himself as the elect one, with humanity chosen in him; and corporate readings, argued by William Klein (The New Chosen People, 1990), stress that ‘us’ is plural, a people chosen in its head. All agree that the verse grounds salvation in God's initiative.

Predestination here is to a family relationship: adoption through Jesus Christ. The contested questions about predestination (see verse 4) should not hide what the verse names as its content and motive: sonship, and God's delight.

On either reading, the verse places God's purpose before history: either the names were written before the world began, or the Lamb's sacrifice was determined then (1 Peter 1:19-20 says he was foreknown before the foundation of the world). Christians who differ on predestination agree that the verse is meant to steady the persecuted, not to make them anxious: those in the Lamb's book are kept from the beast's worship.

The last word of the chapter rests on a book the Lamb holds. The warning is severe, but its point for John's hearers is assurance: those written in the Lamb's book do not share the fate of the dragon and his beasts.
